messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark traced the fire escape route on the building blueprint across the street with his eyes, a familiar exercise he performed from his fourteenth-floor office window. He could name every exit from his own building, knew the turn radius of the stairwells, and had calculated the time it would take to reach the ground floor from his desk. Only after this silent reconnaissance could he turn his attention to the tax codes on his screen. The quiet hum of the office servers was a constant, low-grade hum of dread; he had come to believe that silence was never empty, but was instead the space where a threat gathered itself before striking.

It had been eight years since the ambush outside Kandahar, but the event lived in his senses. Sometimes, a memory would surface with such force that he would have to brace himself against his desk, overwhelmed by a tidal wave of panic and grief. In those moments, the dry, sterile air of his office would fill with the coppery taste of blood and dust, the exact sensation he’d had after the IED detonated, and he would be back in the ringing silence that followed the blast. At other times, the memory was a silent film he watched from a great distance. He could see it all—the overturned vehicle, the smoke, the shouting—but felt nothing, as if he were merely an analyst reviewing footage of a stranger’s catastrophe.

These fragmented returns of the past governed his present. He had built a life of careful, rigid control. At work, this translated into meticulous, sought-after consulting, but it came at a cost. A client raising their voice during a tense discussion about audits could send a jolt of ice through his veins, making him want to flee the room. He would feel the same spike of adrenaline he felt in the moments before the firefight began, when the village elder’s tone had shifted from hospitable to hostile. He now steered all conversations, personal and professional, away from any topic that touched on duty, loyalty, or conflict, leaving colleagues to see him as aloof and impersonal.

At home, the walls he built were even higher. His wife, Sarah, had long ago stopped trying to touch him without announcing her approach from across the room. A simple hand on his shoulder as he read on the sofa could make him leap to his feet, heart hammering, his body reacting to a threat that wasn't there. He saw the hurt in her eyes but couldn't explain the reaction, so he said nothing at all. He knew she felt his distance as a rejection. When she once planned a surprise party for his promotion, he felt a surge of panic, not joy. He couldn't tolerate positive feelings; they felt like a dangerous lapse in vigilance, a foolish indulgence before the inevitable disaster. He retreated to their bedroom for the rest of the evening, leaving her to entertain their friends alone.

Any hint of physical vulnerability was a potent trigger. A common cold or a headache would plunge him into a state of high alert, his mind convinced that his body was failing and that he was exposed, helpless, just as he had been while lying injured and disoriented in the wreckage. He would become irritable and withdrawn, unable to tolerate Sarah’s attempts to care for him. He avoided physical contact not just with her, but with everyone, recoiling from handshakes and sidestepping colleagues in the hallway.

It was after a particularly bad week, when a bout of the flu had left him sleepless and on edge for days, that Sarah finally told him she couldn’t live with the ghost in their house any longer. She didn’t give him an ultimatum, but he heard one in the quiet finality of her voice. Mark is now seeking help because the life he has so carefully constructed is threatening to collapse. He is terrified of talking about what happened, certain that to give it words would be to make it real forever, but a deeper fear has taken root: the fear of losing everything that remains.
